trails.bestSeason: Nov-Apr (cooler, fewer mosquitoes); boat access only
trails.trailTip: This trail follows an old overgrown roadbed on Elliott Key and is reachable only by private boat or the park's seasonal ferry — bring strong insect repellent, since mosquitoes can be intense even in cooler months.
trails.didYouKnow: Spite Highway got its name from a 1960s road-clearing project by developers hoping to subdivide the island, halted when the area became parkland — the cleared swath remains as this trail.

trails.trailTip: A short, flat, paved path from the visitor center to a rock jetty with open bay views — a good easy option for visitors without a boat.
trails.didYouKnow: This is one of the only trails in the park accessible without a boat, since over 95% of Biscayne National Park is open water.

trails.trailTip: A wheelchair-accessible boardwalk over the mangroves right behind the visitor center, good for a quick look at mangrove habitat without a boat trip.
trails.didYouKnow: The mangroves visible from this boardwalk are a nursery habitat for juvenile fish, sharks, and spiny lobsters before they move out to the reef.

trails.trailTip: As of September 2026, per NPS.gov, camping and docking fees at Boca Chita are waived from May 1 through September 30 each year, and sites are first-come, first-served with no advance reservation — pack out everything, since there is no trash service on the island.
trails.didYouKnow: The ornamental lighthouse at Boca Chita was built in the 1930s by Mark Honeywell as a decorative feature for his private retreat and has never functioned as an official aid to navigation.

trails.trailTip: Adams Key is day-use only with no overnight camping — a quiet, short nature walk through what was once a private resort island.
trails.didYouKnow: Adams Key was once home to the Cocolobo Cay Club, a private retreat that hosted several U.S. presidents before the island became parkland.

trails.trailTip: A very short boardwalk loop through red mangroves — good for spotting small fish and crabs in the shallow water beneath the walkway.
trails.didYouKnow: Red mangroves' arching prop roots filter salt and help trap sediment, slowly building new land at the water's edge.

trails.trailTip: A quiet, little-visited path on a small mangrove-fringed key — bring your own drinking water, as there are no facilities on the island.
trails.didYouKnow: Sands Key sits within one of the park's undeveloped barrier-island beach areas used by nesting loggerhead sea turtles each summer.

trails.trailTip: The park's largest key has one of the least-visited trails in the park — tell someone your plan before heading out, since cell service is unreliable and boat traffic to this key is light.
trails.didYouKnow: Totten Key was historically farmed for key limes and pineapples before the land was acquired for the park.

animals.bestSeason: Year-round; more visible in cooler months while basking
animals.whereToLook: Mangrove-lined shallows near Convoy Point and the park's canals
animals.viewingTip: View any crocodile from a boat or the shoreline with binoculars or a zoom lens, and never approach, feed, or try to get closer for a photo — this is a federally protected, potentially dangerous animal, and disturbing it is both unsafe and illegal.
animals.didYouKnow: Biscayne is near the northern edge of the American crocodile's U.S. range and one of only a handful of parks where the species can be reliably found.

animals.bestTimeOfDay: Midday, when sunlight helps spot them near the surface
animals.bestSeason: Nov-Apr (manatees concentrate in warmer, shallow water)
animals.whereToLook: Shallow seagrass flats and channels near the visitor center and canals
animals.viewingTip: Watch quietly from a boat or shoreline with polarized sunglasses and binoculars, keep idle speed and distance in any boat near a surfacing manatee, and never touch or try to swim toward one, even though they appear slow and approachable.
animals.didYouKnow: Manatees must surface to breathe every few minutes and can be spotted by watching for the ripple of a snout or tail breaking the surface.

animals.bestTimeOfDay: Night (nesting females); daytime for feeding turtles offshore
animals.bestSeason: May-Oct (nesting season on the park's outer keys)
animals.whereToLook: Undeveloped beaches on Elliott Key and other barrier islands
animals.viewingTip: View any turtle from a distance and never use flashlights or flash photography near a nesting female or hatchlings on a barrier-island beach — light disorients them and can lead them away from the water.
animals.didYouKnow: A female loggerhead returns to nest on the same general stretch of beach where she herself hatched, sometimes decades earlier.

animals.whereToLook: Nests atop channel markers and dead snags throughout the bay
animals.viewingTip: Watch nesting platforms from a boat at a comfortable distance with binoculars rather than motoring close for a photo, especially during winter nesting season when a disturbed adult may abandon the nest.
animals.didYouKnow: Ospreys plunge feet-first into the water to catch fish and can be seen carrying prey aligned head-first in flight to reduce wind drag.

animals.whereToLook: Seagrass beds and patch reefs accessible by snorkeling tours
animals.viewingTip: Observe parrotfish while snorkeling by keeping a relaxed distance and letting them graze undisturbed — avoid chasing or cornering fish for a closer look, which stresses them and can damage the surrounding reef.
animals.didYouKnow: Parrotfish bite and grind coral to feed on the algae inside it, and their digested coral waste is a major natural source of the white sand found on nearby beaches.

animals.whereToLook: Open bay channels, often visible from tour boats
animals.viewingTip: Watch dolphins from a boat at idle speed and a respectful distance, letting them approach if they choose rather than pursuing or trying to swim with them, per federal marine mammal protection guidelines.
animals.didYouKnow: Bottlenose dolphins in Biscayne Bay have been documented using cooperative feeding strategies, herding fish into shallow mud banks together.

animals.whereToLook: Sandy flats and seagrass beds visible from boats or while snorkeling
animals.viewingTip: Watch eagle rays glide over the seagrass from a boat or while snorkeling at a distance, using a mask and fins rather than free-diving down toward one for a closer look.
animals.didYouKnow: Spotted eagle rays can leap fully out of the water, a behavior thought to help them shake off parasites or possibly communicate.

animals.bestTimeOfDay: Daytime for feeding turtles; night for nesting females
animals.whereToLook: Seagrass meadows throughout the bay, and outer key beaches during nesting season
animals.viewingTip: Watch feeding turtles from a boat or while snorkeling without chasing or touching them, and on a nesting beach at night keep well back, skip flash photography and white light, and let a nesting female or emerging hatchlings finish undisturbed.
animals.didYouKnow: Green sea turtles are named for the color of their body fat, not their shell — a result of their mostly plant-based diet of seagrass and algae.
